prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

No remembering now when the apple sapling was blown almost out of the ground. No telling how, with all the other trees around, it alone was struck. It must have been luck, he thought for years, so close to the house it grew. It must have been night. Change is a thing one sleeps through when young, and he was young. If there was a weakness in the earth, a give he went down on his knees to find and feel the limits of, there is no longer. If there was one random blow from above the way he's come to know from years in this place, the roots were stronger. Whatever the case, he has watched this tree survive wind ripping at his roof for nights on end, heats and blights that left little else alive. No remembering now... A day's changes mean all to him and all days come down to one clear pane through which he sees among all the other trees this leaning, clenched, unyielding one that seems cast in the form of a blast that would have killed it, as if something at the heart of things, and with the heart of things, had willed it.

Here are three refined versions, ranging from a polished literary style to a sleek, modern prose style. All options preserve the original narrative, imagery, and information.

### Option 1: Elegant & Poetic (Recommended)
*This version retains the rhythmic, atmospheric quality of the original while elevating the diction and seamlessness of the prose.*

> He can no longer recall when the apple sapling was nearly uprooted from the earth, nor explain how, amidst a surrounding stand of trees, it alone was struck. For years, he attributed its survival to fortune, growing as close to the house as it did. It must have happened in the night—for change is something one sleeps through in youth, and he was young then. If the earth once harbored a weakness—a yield he had dropped to his knees to trace and measure—it does so no longer. If it suffered a random blow from above, the likes of which he has come to recognize through decades in this place, its roots proved the stronger force. 
>
> In any case, he has watched this tree endure relentless winds that tore at his roof for nights on end, along with severe heats and blights that left little else alive. Time has blurred the past; now, the subtle changes of a single day mean everything to him. All his days ultimately converge at a single, clear windowpane. Through it, set against every other tree, he beholds this leaning, clenched, unyielding survivor—frozen in the very shape of the blast that should have destroyed it, as if something at the very heart of nature had profoundly willed its endurance.

---

### Option 2: Sophisticated & Fluid
*This option streamlines the cadence for maximum clarity and narrative momentum while keeping a literary tone.*

> He no longer remembers when the apple sapling was almost torn from the ground, nor can he explain why it alone was struck among all the neighboring trees. Growing so close to the house, he assumed for years it was simply luck. It must have occurred at night; youth sleeps through change, and he was young. If there was ever a softness in the soil—a give he once fell to his knees to measure—it is gone now. If it took a sudden strike from above, of the kind he has grown accustomed to over years on this land, the roots ultimately prevailed. 
>
> Whatever transpired, he has watched this tree survive tempestuous winds that rattled his roof for days, as well as scorching heat and blights that decimated the surrounding landscape. He remembers little of those early years now. Today, a single day’s shift holds immense meaning, and all his days come down to one clear pane of glass. Looking out, amidst all the other trees, he sees this leaning, clenched, indomitable trunk. It stands cast in the exact form of the blast that sought to kill it, as though a force at the core of all things had willed it to remain.

---

*   **Syntax & Rhythm:** Fixed the conversational fragments (e.g., "No remembering now," "It must have been night") into complete, evocative sentences that flow naturally.
*   **Elevated Diction:** Replaced repetitive phrasing (like "heats and blights") with richer descriptive terms ("scorching heat and blights," "severe heats").
*   **Enhanced Ending:** Preserved the poetic cadence of the closing thought ("killed it / willed it") by crafting a smooth, powerful final cadence.

The exact moment a young apple tree was nearly ripped from the soil has long faded from memory. It remains impossible to explain why, out of the entire surrounding grove, this solitary plant was the only one targeted. For decades, he attributed its survival to sheer fortune, given how close it stood to his home. The event undoubtedly occurred after dark; major transformations often happen while the young are asleep, and he was just a boy at the time. Although he once got down on his hands and knees to feel the boundaries of the loosened dirt around it, that instability has completely vanished. If a sudden, violent tempest had struck it—a phenomenon he has grown deeply familiar with over a lifetime spent on this land—the tree's subterranean network proved the stronger force. 

Regardless of the specifics, he has repeatedly watched this tree endure relentless gales that tore at his roof tiles for nights on end, as well as scorching droughts and infections that wiped out nearly all surrounding life. Those initial details are forgotten now. Instead, every minor daily shift holds immense significance for him, with all his days ultimately centering on a single transparent windowpane. Looking out through the glass into the woods, he observes this solitary, slanted, tightly bound, and stubborn tree. Its very shape appears permanently molded by the destructive force that should have ended it, as if some fundamental impulse at the very core of reality had deliberately commanded it to endure.

When the man was still a boy, a ferocious storm swept across the land near his childhood home, threatening to tear apart everything in its path. Standing vulnerable in the yard was a young apple sapling, its slender trunk whipped violently by the howling winds. The gale raged with terrifying force, and for hours, it seemed as though the fragile sapling would be completely uprooted and swept away.

The odds were stacked against the small tree. The surrounding soil was loose and saturated by rain, offering precious little natural support against such a violent tempest. Yet, hidden beneath the mud, the sapling’s roots were far stronger than anyone realized. Deep beneath the surface, they coiled tightly around the earth, holding fast through the fury of the night and refusing to let go.

Decades passed, and the relentless seasons brought a continuous cycle of hardship. The apple tree faced bitter winter gales, scorching summer heatwaves, and destructive blights that ravaged the surrounding landscape, destroying much of the local plant life. While larger trees snapped and delicate greenery withered away, the apple tree stubbornly held its ground, surviving every trial that nature cast its way.

Today, the mature tree bears the distinct mark of its lifelong struggle. It stands permanently leaning and tightly clenched, forever shaped by the trajectory of that original, terrifying blast from his youth. It never grew perfectly upright, but its stooped, gnarled frame is not a sign of weakness; it is the physical architecture of survival.

Now, as an older man, he often looks out his window to gaze at the battered tree standing quietly in the yard. In its bent branches and deeply anchored trunk, he sees more than just an old plant. To him, the tree remains a quiet, unyielding testament to deep, enduring resilience—a daily reminder of the quiet strength required to withstand life's greatest storms.
outputs.L4:
For nearly forty years, my mornings have begun at the same kitchen window, looking out across the gentle incline of the eastern meadow. And every morning, my eyes land on the same singular presence: a wild apple tree that defies every law of symmetry and poise.

It stands—or rather, leans—at an improbable, acute angle, as though caught in a perpetual tilt toward the horizon. To a passerby, it looks like a creature mid-fall, frozen by some sudden magic. But to me, who has watched it through four decades of shifting light and changing seasons, that desperate slant is not a sign of imminent collapse. It is the very monument of its survival.

I was a young man when the blast occurred. It happened on a silent, moonless night in late autumn—a sound like the earth tearing open, accompanied by a brief, blinding flash of violet light that shook the glass in my windowpanes. By dawn, the source remained a mystery; there was no crater, no wreckage, no fallen meteor. There was only a scorch mark across the grass and, at its epicenter, the young apple sapling I had planted just two years prior. 

The little tree had been devastated. Its slender trunk was bent almost flush to the ground, its young leaves carbonized to ash, and its delicate roots pulled taut and exposed to the biting morning frost. It looked irreparably ruined, a fragile thing crushed by an arbitrary bolt of violence. I almost brought an axe to it that afternoon to spare it the slow misery of dying. 

Yet, I hesitated. Something in the way the snapped fibers of its trunk held on made me leave it alone. I heaped fresh earth over its exposed roots, left it to the cold, and expected the winter to finish what the fire had started.

Winter came, bringing months of shrieking gales and heavy, wet snow that buried the sapling entirely. But when the melt arrived in April, a miracle unfolded in miniature. Along the undersides of the broken, slanted stem, small green buds began to push through the scarred wood. 

Over the decades that followed, I watched the sapling transform into a quiet battleground of life versus gravity. It never straightened. The violent force that had struck it in its youth had permanently rewritten its posture. Instead of reaching straight toward the heavens like the oaks at the edge of the woods, the apple tree grew outward at a forty-five-degree angle. 

To compensate, its anatomy changed in extraordinary ways. The roots on the side opposite the lean broadened into thick, wooden buttresses, plunging deep into the rocky soil like anchors thrown into a stormy sea. The bark along its underside thickened, forming heavy, braided ridges of scar tissue that supported the immense weight of its horizontal reach. Every harsh winter, every summer drought, every punishing gale that swept through the valley seemed only to harden its resolve. The weather tried to push it over, but the tree simply used the tension to anchor itself deeper.

Today, the sapling is a fully mature tree. Its bark is gnarled, moss-draped, and deeply furrowed, bearing the indelible imprint of the night it was nearly destroyed. Yet every spring, without fail, its lopsided canopy erupts into a cloud of fragrant, pale-pink blossoms. Every autumn, its branches bend low under the weight of small, tart red apples—fruit that tastes sweeter, I often think, for the hardship that birthed it.

I am an old man now, my own body beginning to stoop and ache with the weight of time. When I look out at the apple tree, I no longer see a victim of a long-ago disaster. I see a profound, almost conscious stubbornness—a silent declaration that life does not merely endure calamity, but molds itself around it. The tree was not broken by the blast; it was shaped by it. It stands as a testament to a deep, obstinate will buried at the very heart of nature, proving that even when we are bent to the very brink of the earth, we can still learn to bloom.
outputs.L5:
**The Power of "Whatever": Finding Peace in Constant Change**

Change is the only true constant in life, yet human beings spend an exhausting amount of energy fighting it. We build routines, cling to plans, and construct delicate illusions of control. But eventually, the wind shifts. A job ends, a relationship evolves, a global event redirects our path, or a simple rainy day ruins a long-awaited trip. When faced with these inevitable disruptions, we are given a choice in how we react. We can rage against the storm, or we can adopt a surprisingly profound philosophy captured in a single, often-misunderstood word: *Whatever*.

At first glance, "whatever" sounds like the motto of apathy—a shrug of teenage indifference, a dismissive wave of the hand, or a sign of giving up. But when applied intentionally to the reality of change, "whatever" transforms into a superpower. It becomes the ultimate expression of radical acceptance. 

To embrace "whatever" in the face of change is not to stop caring; it is to stop clinging. It is the realization that while we cannot control the weather of life, we can choose not to let it ruin our day. When a carefully crafted plan crumbles, a rigid mindset breaks under the pressure. A flexible mindset, however, simply shrugs and says, *"Whatever comes next, I will handle it."*

This mindset shifts us from resistance to resilience. Change forces us to pivot, and "whatever" gives us the permission to do so without bitterness. Missed the train? *Whatever, I’ll read a book while I wait for the next one.* The career path took an unexpected detour? *Whatever, let’s see what new skills I can learn here.* 

Life is an unpredictable, ever-shifting landscape. We can spend our lives mourning the landscapes we’ve left behind, or we can look at the uncharted territory ahead and greet it with a peaceful, open-minded "whatever." In the end, change will happen whether we consent to it or not. Mastering the art of "whatever" ensures that no matter how drastically the world changes around us, our inner peace remains entirely our own.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of poetic prose about an old man reflecting on a resilient apple tree that survived a terrible storm in his youth.
counterfactuals.output:
He traces the parchment of his own knuckles, listening to the orchard breathe in the quiet twilight. There, at the edge of the clearing, stands the old apple tree—leaning, gnarled, and defiant against the darkening sky.

His mind drifts back sixty years, to a night when the world unraveled. He remembers the storm not as weather, but as a ravenous beast, howling down from the mountains, tearing the shingles from the roof and spitting hail like broken teeth. He had been a young man then, pressed against the windowpane, trembling as the darkness swallowed the valley. Through the flashes of jagged violet light, he had watched the young tree fight for its life. It bent double, its green boughs whipped into a frenzied dance, screaming against a wind that sought to erase it. When a heavy main limb snapped with a sound like a rifle shot, the boy had buried his face in his hands, certain the tree was lost.

But the morning arrived washed clean and terrifyingly still. 

He had walked out into the ruined yard through debris and uprooted saplings. The apple tree remained. It was battered, stripped of leaves, and bleeding sweet sap from a jagged, weeping wound where its limb had torn away. Yet its roots held fast, anchored deep in the dark, stubborn earth. It had refused to fall.

Now, the old man smiles, a slow warming of his wintered face. Over the decades, he watched the tree heal. It grew crooked around its scar, weaving new wood over old agony, turning its hurt into a knee of solid bark. And every spring, without fail, it crowned itself in soft, defiant pink blossoms. Every autumn, it offered fruit—sweeter, it seemed, for the hardship it had endured.

He leans heavily on his cane, feeling the weight of his own long years, the invisible scars he carries from his own forgotten tempests. He looks across the grass at his old friend. They are both gnarled now, both bent by time, but both still standing, bathed in the quiet grace of having survived.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a literary flash fiction piece focusing on themes of time, youth, memory, and survival in nature. Structure it around an old apple tree near a house that grew sideways after a storm, written with repetitive phrases like "No remembering now."
counterfactuals.output:
The gale of ’84 laid the apple tree flat, or nearly flat, snapping its spine at a cruel forty-five degrees and pinning its highest leaves into the mud. But the roots held. The wood refused to rot. It hardened into a thick, horizontal elbow, lifting its remaining boughs parallel to the grass, a green spine crawling inches above the dirt toward the porch of the weatherboard house.

No remembering now the night the sky broke. 

No remembering now the roar of the gale, the crack of heartwood, the terrible dark weight of the storm.

The tree survived by altering its geometry. Where it had once aimed for the sun in a straight, arrogant spire, it now crept sideways like an old dog seeking a patch of light. It bore fruit along its belly. Children used the slanted trunk as a balance beam, running its length with bare, dirty feet, their youth loud and reckless against the silent patience of the bark.

No remembering now those small, fast feet. 

No remembering now the girl with bruised knees who sat astride the bend, spitting black seeds into the tall clover, promising the sky she would never leave this yard. 

Decades pooled in the grass beneath the low branches like standing rain. The children grew up and away, pulled by the far-off currents of the world, their laughter thinning into silence, their faces blurred by the slow rust of time. The house behind the tree grew gray, its white paint peeling off in ribbons, its windows staring blankly out at the orchard’s lone survivor. 

Only the tree stayed, stubborn and bent, its bark scarred where the lightning had licked it, its leaves still turning silver before a summer rain. 

No remembering now the sweet, unblemished apples of its youth. 

Only the sour, knotty fruit of its endurance remained—small, hard spheres that tasted of cold well-water and old soil, falling softly into the deep grass every October, ungathered, unpeeled, untouched. 

Inside the house, an old woman moves slowly behind the glass. Her mind is a clear room emptied of furniture, swept clean by the quiet drift of years. She looks out at the yard, at the strange, crooked miracle resting in the weeds. She does not know who planted it. She does not know who climbed it.

No remembering now the storm. 

No remembering now the girl.

Outside, the tree swells with autumn sap, pressing its heavy, sideways body into the earth, surviving simply because it knows no other way to meet the morning light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a gnarled tree that refused to die, written from the perspective of someone aging alongside it.
counterfactuals.output:
The arborists called it a hazard thirty years ago. They pointed to the gaping cavity in its flank, the stark grey split where lightning had split its core during the heatwave of ’82, and said it was only a matter of time. 

I told them to pack up their chainsaws and leave. I think, even then, I knew I was defending my own future.

Now, I sit on the porch with a wool blanket draped over knees that no longer bend without complaining, and I look at it across the yard. We are a matching pair, that old bur oak and I—two stubborn monuments to surviving past our prime.

It doesn’t grow straight like the young maples by the driveway, which shoot toward the sky with the smooth, unburdened arrogance of youth. The oak is a twisted fist of a tree. Its trunk swerving violently to the left near the base, a calcified dodge against some long-forgotten shadow, before surging upward in a series of jagged knots and burls. Its bark is thick and deeply furrowed, dark as wet earth, resembling the heavy, sun-leathered creases on the backs of my own hands. 

Half of its crown is pure grey bone—dead wood that rattles when the November gales blow down from the ridge. Any right-minded organism would have surrendered when the ice storm of ’98 snapped its lowest boughs, or when the rot took hold of its heartwood. But the oak simply pinched off the dead pathways and routed its life somewhere else. 

I know the feeling. My own heart has lost a chamber or two to grief; my lungs don't draw the deep, effortless draughts they used to. Yet, the sap still rises.

Every spring, when the rest of the valley blooms in a rush of pastel vanity, the old tree waits. It lets the foolish young saplings risk their early leaves to the late frosts. Only when May is certain does it push out its offerings: not a lush, symmetrical canopy, but dense, fierce clusters of deep green leaves erupting from the unlikeliest places. Leaves sprout directly from the scarred trunk, out of the dead rot, clinging to the shattered arm of the lightning strike. It is an ugly, beautiful defiance. 

Yesterday, my granddaughter offered to help me up the porch steps. She held my elbow with the soft, terrified gentleness people reserve for things they expect to break. I let her, but once I was in my chair, I looked out at the oak. 

One of its heaviest boughs has bowed so low over the decades that it now rests directly on the earth, using the ground as a crutch, before curving back up toward the sun. It found a way to bear its own weight when the trunk grew too tired to hold it alone. 

I rested my cane against my leg and smiled at the sight of it. 

The frost will come for both of us eventually. The winter will arrive that we cannot thaw out of, and the wind will finally catch us at the precise angle needed to lay us down. But until that day, we have a silent pact, that tree and I. We do not ask to be pretty. We do not ask to be whole. We simply grip the earth with our crooked roots, soak up whatever light the afternoon gives us, and flatly refuse to go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic vignette about a man looking out his window at a crooked apple tree. Explore the idea that the storm which almost destroyed the tree actually gave it its permanent, unyielding shape, as if fate willed its survival.
counterfactuals.output:
The glass was cool against his forehead, keeping the twilight at a gentle distance. Outside, framed perfectly by the dark wood of the window, the apple tree pitched hard toward the east, frozen in a low, stubborn bow. It was not a grand tree by any traditional measure—not tall, nor symmetrical, but gnarled and low-slung, its trunk a thick coil of grey iron wood, its branches reaching out not upward, but sideways, like a runner braced against a wind that had passed decades ago.

He remembered the night the geometry of the yard had changed. It was a late-autumn tempest that had torn the sky into ragged black ribbons. Standing at this same pane, he had watched the young tree whip violently in the dark, a slender thing fighting a force that wanted only to level the earth. A sickening crack had echoed above the gale, and by morning, the sapling was bent nearly double, its bark split, its roots strained to white knuckles beneath the mud. It had looked ruined—a victim waiting for the rot to finish what the storm had begun.

Yet the sap had not stopped running. 

Season by season, the tree refused the gravity of its ruin. The torn wood calloused over into a thick, silvery seam. Instead of straightening, it grew dense along the curve, laying down ring after tight ring of hardened grain in the very angle of its breaking. The storm had not snapped the tree; it had forged it. The gale had acted like a sculptor’s heavy mallet, striking away the fragile, upright innocence to reveal an unyielding hook of muscle beneath. 

Fate had not willed the tree to be spared the blow. It had willed the blow to become the tree's permanent spine.

Now, straight oaks in the distance shuddered at every minor squall, but the crooked apple tree never moved. It was already shaped like the storm. It bore its heavy, sun-freckled fruit on branches that hovered just above the grass, holding its impossible posture with a quiet, defiant grace. 

The man exhaled, his breath fogging a small circle on the glass, momentarily blurring the wild shape outside. When the mist cleared, the tree remained—crooked, rooted, and entirely unbroken.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
